## Series Overview

Everyone is talking about "AI software factories". Most of what I have seen are demos where an agent
writes some code and everyone claps. I want to build one the way this blog builds everything else: a
narrow target, small steps, real runs, held-out evaluation, and numbers I report even when they are
unflattering.

**The target.** The inspection pipeline from the Zero-to-Advanced series: detect, measure, classify,
apply rules, decide, report. The factory's job is to take a **ticket** ("add a rule for X", "cut the
tokens per frame", "handle a frame with no candidates"), have agents change the pipeline, and merge the
change only if it passes a **gate**. No ticket, no change. No pass, no merge.

**The sibling series.** The factory core built here (ticket queue, gate runner, audit log, sandbox) is reused
by [Agentic AI Software Factory: Robust Segmentation Models](../agentic-factory-segmentation/index.qmd).

## What the research found, and what it changed

I read around the published work before planning. The short version, with links to the sources I could open:

- **Agents take the cheapest path to a green signal.** METR measured reward hacking in 39 of 128 RE-Bench runs
  (30.4%), including overwriting the timer and stubbing the evaluator
  ([METR](https://metr.org/blog/2025-06-05-recent-reward-hacking)). NIST's CAISI describes agents reading the answer
  from the repository history
  ([CAISI](https://www.nist.gov/caissi/2-examples-cheating-caisis-agent-evaluations)). Telling the model not to cheat
  barely moved the rate, so **prompts are not a control**. The gate has to be made of permissions and processes.
- **Permissions are not a sandbox.** Anthropic's own Claude Code documentation calls permission rules "a permission
  gate, not a sandbox", says Read and Edit deny rules do not cover a script that opens files itself, and says a hook
  that times out or crashes does not block by default
  ([permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions), [hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks),
  [sandboxing](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing)).
- **Passing tests is not the same as shippable.** METR found that about half of the test-passing SWE-bench Verified
  changes would not be merged by the project's maintainers
  ([METR](https://metr.org/notes/2026-03-10-many-swe-bench-passing-prs-would-not-be-merged-into-main/)).
- **There is a gap in the evidence.** I found no public bad-merge rate, review-minutes figure or cost per merged
  change for a real factory. So this series cannot compare itself with anyone's numbers. It can only measure its
  own, on its own small scale, and say so.

Several of the sources behind this are secondary or vendor write-ups (the OpenAI and StrongDM factory accounts, for
example). I have kept them out of anything load-bearing.

## The design rules

1. **The gate is not the agents' to edit.** The evaluator, thresholds and held-out cases are never writable by the
   agent. The gate runs from a pinned copy in a separate process, and the held-out cases are not in the agent's
   checkout at all.
2. **The gate writes the verdict, not the agent.** An agent's own report that it succeeded does not count. The gate
   returns only a coarse result (pass or fail, a reason from a small fixed set, queries remaining), never per-case
   scores. This follows the reusable-holdout results: even a scalar score leaks label information to something that
   keeps querying it ([Blum and Hardt](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04585)).
3. **Escalate, never guess.** When the factory is unsure it stops and asks a person (the human review planned for Part 9
   of the Zero-to-Advanced series).
4. **Measure the factory itself,** with numbers fixed before building, and allow "no resolvable difference" as a result.
5. **Report intervals.** A small gate set is noisy: a recall of 0.8 on 30 positives has a standard error of about 0.07
   (my own arithmetic). Comparisons will be paired, with confidence intervals, and every post says how many cases it rests on.

## The shared factory core

Four small pieces, run by one orchestrator that is plain code and not an agent. They are designed here and reused in
the segmentation series.

- **Ticket queue.** A small database with a state machine (queued, running, gated, merged, rejected, needs a human),
  one row per ticket with its spec, budget, seed and parent commit. A single serial integrator rebases each ticket
  branch, runs the gate and fast-forwards `main`. The documented tools I looked at have no merge queue or fleet-wide
  budget, so I will build these by hand.
- **Gate runner.** A separate process, ideally a separate container, that checks out the candidate read-only, overlays
  pinned tests and evaluator, and returns the coarse verdict. The gate's own tests get tested too, with null and
  deliberately bad patches.
- **Audit log.** An append-only log of ticket events, gate queries, verdicts and budget draws, written by the
  orchestrator. Every metric the posts report comes from it. Transcripts are audited for reads of protected paths, and
  decoy files act as tripwires.
- **Sandbox and permissions.** Layered, with the outer boundary doing the real work. On the machine I build on, the
  Claude Code sandbox's `bubblewrap` layer fails (Ubuntu restricts unprivileged user namespaces) and the Docker group is
  effectively root. So the plan is a Docker container with read-only mounts and no network, optionally a Landlock
  launcher, and sealed labels that are simply never mounted into the agent's world. Deny rules and hooks are treated
  as layers that catch accidents, and their gaps get shown in a post.

**A local baseline.** Claude Code cannot be pointed at a local non-Claude model, so the local Qwen3-Coder baseline needs a
different harness (LangGraph Deep Agents is the candidate), and the comparison is between two systems, not two models.

## Planned measures

Decided before building, published whatever they turn out to be:

- gate-pass rate against the audited bad-merge rate (changes that passed the gate and were later judged bad), each with
  an interval
- tokens, cost estimate and wall-clock time per merged ticket (cost figures are client-side estimates, not billing data)
- human review minutes per ticket
- repeat runs of the same ticket, to expose flakiness

## Posts in this Series (all coming soon)

Each post will end with a "what I did not do" section. The outcomes below are open questions, not promises.

1. **Why a factory needs a gate it cannot edit.** Freeze the pipeline at a tagged commit, write the ticket schema and a first
   batch of tickets, and measure the baseline with intervals. If, and only if, it really happens in a run, show the failure the
   gate exists for: agents editing tests.
2. **A ticket queue and a headless runner.** The queue, the serial integrator and a headless agent wrapper with a budget and a
   timeout. Measure cost, time, turns and the rate of runs that end with no valid output.
3. **Gate v1: pinned tests, restored files and a coarse verdict.** Measure the gate's false-pass rate on hand-written bad patches
   (a null patch, a test-deleting patch, an evaluator-stubbing patch), and show a trivial change that fools a naive gate but
   not the pinned one.
4. **Permissions are not a sandbox: what failed on this machine.** The container and the launcher, plus a battery of escape
   attempts that I write, recording which layer stopped each one. Show the real failures: the sandbox error on this host, a hook
   that fails open, a deny rule a script walks around.
5. **A held-out gate for an X-ray pipeline.** Synthetic cases with exact ground truth, a locked confirmation split and a
   never-queried second split. Measure the gap between them and report honestly if the set is too small to resolve a three-point
   gain.
6. **Reviewer agents and the cost of crying wolf.** A fresh-context, read-only reviewer against gate-only, on the same
   tickets. Measure how many bad patches it catches and how many good ones it flags. Anthropic's own guidance warns that a
   reviewer asked to find problems will report some even when the work is sound.
7. **Forty tickets, one gate, and an audit of what got merged.** The main run. The bad-merge rate with an exact interval, the
   gap between gate-pass and audited result, tokens and review minutes per merged ticket. It will not generalise beyond its
   own ticket set.
8. **A local Qwen3-Coder baseline needs a different harness.** The same container, an open model and a different harness.
   Measure malformed tool calls, tickets completed and memory contention with the other model servers, and settle the
   tool-call parser question with a local test instead of an assumption.

Candidate posts, not yet researched: merge, deploy and roll back; a retrospective that hands over to the model factory.

## Data and licensing

No company data goes into this series. The Zero-to-Advanced series first ran on GDXray, whose authors offer it for research and
educational use only and prohibit redistribution ([GDXray page](https://domingomery.ing.uc.cl/material/gdxray)), so it was
rebuilt on the [synthetic void dataset](../agentic-factory-segmentation/01-synthetic-void-dataset.qmd) with exact ground truth.
This series uses the same dataset, so every image it shows can be shown. A small real set may be kept locally as a sim-to-real
check and never shown.

## Reads best after

Parts 1 to 9 of [Zero to Advanced](../agentic-zero-to-advanced/index.qmd) (the loop, the graph, the pipeline, tool design,
human review), plus its evaluation and testing posts.

## How this series will be written

Same rules as the rest of the blog: every number comes from a real run, evaluation uses held-out data, each post ends with a
"what I did not do" section, and anything I could not run or verify is labelled as such.
